How much CO₂ does C-201 emit, and where does it come from?

Lecture 1-1 · the plan

From levers to one baseline number

  1. The levers on the mapwhich decarbonization pillars a single process unit can pull
  2. Counting in CO₂eglobal warming potential turns every gas into one number
  3. Where a unit's emissions sitScope 1, 2 and 3, and the steam boundary

From Lecture 12, Decarbonization technologies (Dr. Pramote Puengjinda, German agency for international cooperation (GIZ))

Five pillars, one order of attack

Energy sufficiency and efficiency come first; renewable power and electrification next; green molecules (hydrogen and power-to-X, PtX) only where the first four cannot reach.

IRENA World Energy Transitions Outlook 2023, 1.5 °C scenario

Half of the 2050 cut is efficiency and renewables

The pillars give the order. The International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA) gives the weights.

A process engineer moves the efficiency and electrification shares directly, inside the unit.

Renewables, hydrogen and carbon capture reach the unit through the site utilities.

Counting in one currency

Global warming potential turns every gas into CO₂e

Before ranking measures we need one unit to count every greenhouse gas (GHG) in.

$m_i$
mass of greenhouse gas $i$ emitted
g or kg
$\mathrm{GWP}_i$
global warming potential: warming over 100 years per kg, relative to CO₂
–
$m_{\mathrm{CO_2e}}$
CO₂-equivalent mass of the whole release
g or kg
$$m_{\mathrm{CO_2e}}=\sum_i m_i\,\mathrm{GWP}_i$$

GWP values come from IPCC assessment reports: AR5 gives CH₄ 28, N₂O 265.

Example 1.1 · problem statement

EXAMPLE 1.1CO₂-equivalent of a mixed release

Read first

How do you calculate the grams of CO₂ equivalent from an activity that emits 20 grams of methane, 2 grams of nitrous oxide, and 300 grams of carbon dioxide?

Lecture 12, Decarbonization technologies, page 8.

GasMass emitted (g)GWP (AR5)
CO₂3001
CH₄2028
N₂O2265

Example 1.1 · solution

EXAMPLE 1.1Weight each gas by its GWP

From the previous slide$m_{\mathrm{CO_2e}}=\sum_i m_i\,\mathrm{GWP}_i$
$m_{\mathrm{CO_2e}}=300(1)+20(28)+2(265)$each mass times its AR5 GWP
$m_{\mathrm{CO_2e}}=300+560+530=1{,}390\ \mathrm{g\ CO_2e}$sum: CH₄ and N₂O outweigh the CO₂

With AR6 values (fossil CH₄ 29.8, N₂O 273) the same release is 1,442 g: always state the GWP set.

Interactive — drag the sliders

Small methane, large CO₂e

Example 1.1$m_{\mathrm{CO_2e}}=\sum_i m_i\,\mathrm{GWP}_i$
g CO₂e for the release

A gram of methane counts as 28–30 g of CO₂: small leaks of CH₄ can outweigh a large CO₂ stream.

Interactive — C-201 stream 7

Why the vent goes to fuel gas, not to air

Stream 7 carries 1.90 kmol/h of non-condensables (taken as methane, 30.5 kg/h) through PV-210.

Combustion$\mathrm{CH_4+2O_2\rightarrow CO_2+2H_2O}$
burned → CO₂
released CH₄ as CO₂e
total, kg CO₂e/h

Burning 1 kg CH₄ makes 2.75 kg CO₂; releasing it counts 28: a vent to atmosphere is ten times worse than a vent to fuel gas.

Where emissions are reported

Scope 1, 2, 3 — and where steam lands

Scope 1 · direct

Fuel burned on site: the boiler raising C-201's steam, the vent burned as fuel gas.

Scope 2 · bought energy

Grid power for the pumps; steam bought from a neighbour's cogeneration plant.

Scope 3 · value chain

Producing the LPG feed, transporting products, making the equipment.

From utility meter to CO₂

Steam carries the CO₂ of the fuel that raised itstep 1 of 2

C-201 burns nothing itself. Its CO₂ arrives inside the steam, so we need kg CO₂ per kg of steam.

$\Delta h_s$
enthalpy the boiler adds: steam minus boiler feed water
kJ/kg
$\eta_b$
boiler efficiency on lower heating value (LHV)
–
$EF_f$
fuel emission factor per unit of fuel energy
kg CO₂/GJ
$EF_s$
steam emission factor
kg CO₂/kg
$q_f=\dfrac{\Delta h_s}{\eta_b}$fuel energy burned per kg of steam
$EF_s=q_f\,EF_f=\dfrac{\Delta h_s}{\eta_b}\,EF_f$each GJ of fuel carries $EF_f$ kg CO₂

From utility meter to CO₂

0.147 kg CO₂ in every kg of LP steamstep 2 of 2

From the previous slide$EF_s=\dfrac{\Delta h_s}{\eta_b}\,EF_f$
$\Delta h_s=2752-440=2312\ \mathrm{kJ/kg}$saturated 0.45 MPa g steam; feed water 105 °C
$q_f=2312/0.88=2627\ \mathrm{kJ/kg}=2.627\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{GJ/kg}$$\eta_b=0.88$ assumed for a gas boiler
$EF_s=2.627\times10^{-3}\times56.1=0.1474\ \mathrm{kg\,CO_2/kg}$natural gas, IPCC 2006 default

Header 0.45 MPa g from the heat and material balance (HMB); other inputs are assumptions.

From utility meter to CO₂

Electricity: the TGO grid factor

$P_e$
electric power drawn by the unit's motors
kW
$EF_g$
grid emission factor, Scope 2
kg CO₂e/kWh
$$\dot E_e=P_e\,EF_g,\qquad EF_g=0.4750$$

Thailand Greenhouse Gas Management Organization (TGO) value for Scope 2, effective 1 January 2026.

C-201 motors: P-201A 49.7 kW and P-202A 20.7 kW shaft (HMB), motor efficiency 0.93; cooling-water pump 38.7 kW assumed.

Example 1.2 · problem statement

EXAMPLE 1.2The C-201 baseline

Read first

Using the design case of the C-201 heat and material balance (DC3-V1-PE-HMB-001 Rev 0), estimate (a) the unit's emission rate in kg CO₂e/h, (b) its intensity per tonne of feed, (c) the annual emission for 8,000 h, and (d) the share that comes from steam.

Take $EF_s=0.1474$ kg CO₂/kg steam, $EF_g=0.4750$ kg CO₂e/kWh, motor efficiency 0.93, and a cooling-water pump of 38.7 kW.

HMB itemValue
Steam to E-201 (stream 9)5,817 kg/h
Steam to E-203 (stream 10)3,790 kg/h
P-201A / P-202A shaft49.7 / 20.7 kW
Feed (stream 1)31,809 kg/h

DC-PFD-200, design point of the simulator.

Example 1.2 · solution

EXAMPLE 1.2Steam and power, line by linestep 1 of 2

Steam and grid factors$\dot E=\dot m_s\,EF_s+P_e\,EF_g$
$\dot m_s=5817+3790=9607\ \mathrm{kg/h}$both LP steam users
$\dot m_s EF_s=9607\times0.1474=1416\ \mathrm{kg/h}$steam CO₂
$P_e=\dfrac{49.7+20.7}{0.93}+38.7=114.4\ \mathrm{kW}$shaft to electric, plus cooling water
$P_e EF_g=114.4\times0.4750=54.3\ \mathrm{kg/h}$Scope 2 power

Example 1.2 · solution

EXAMPLE 1.21.47 t CO₂e per hour, 96 % from steamstep 2 of 2

From step 1$\dot m_s EF_s=1416,\quad P_e EF_g=54.3\ \mathrm{kg/h}$
$\dot E=1416+54.3=1470\ \mathrm{kg\,CO_2e/h}$(a) emission rate
$I=1470/31.809=46.2\ \mathrm{kg\,CO_2e/t\ feed}$(b) per tonne of feed
$1470\times8000/1000=11{,}760\ \mathrm{t/yr}$(c) annual
$1416/1470=96.3\,\%$(d) steam share

Lecture 1-1 · summary

What section 1-1 settled

  • CO₂e weights each gas by its GWP; state AR5 or AR6.
  • Steam carries its boiler's CO₂: $EF_s=\Delta h_s EF_f/\eta_b=0.147$ kg/kg.
  • C-201 emits about 1,470 kg CO₂e/h, 46 kg per tonne of feed.
  • 96 % comes from steam, so heat is where decarbonization starts.

1-2

Lecture 1-2

How far can better operation cut the steam without new hardware?

Lecture 1-2 · the plan

Energy sufficiency: use only what the spec needs

  1. Where the heat goesthe unit energy balance closes on the condenser
  2. Reflux is steameach m³/h of reflux costs about 49 kW of reboil
  3. Specification giveaway1.5 mol % made against 2.5 mol % allowed
  4. Column pressurelower is easier to separate, limited by the condenser
  5. Pumps and drivesreal savings, but small next to steam

Where the heat goes · HMB design case

Two heaters in, one condenser out

$$Q_{201}+Q_{203}=Q_{202}+\Delta\dot H_{\mathrm{prod}}$$

$Q$ = exchanger duty (kW); $\Delta\dot H_{\mathrm{prod}}$ = enthalpy leaving in products minus feed.

Most steam heat leaves through the condenser to cooling water.

Reflux is steam

One more unit of reflux, one more unit of boil-upstep 1 of 2

The condenser removes what the reboiler boils. So reflux, which the condenser must condense, is paid for in steam.

$L,\ D$
reflux and distillate flows
kg/h
$V$
vapour to the condenser, $V=L+D$
kg/h
$\lambda$
heat removed per kg condensed
kJ/kg
$Q_{202}=V\lambda=(L+D)\lambda$total condenser: all overhead vapour condenses
$\Delta Q_{203}\approx\Delta Q_{202}=\Delta L\,\lambda$feed state and $D$ fixed: boil-up tracks $V$

Reflux is steam

About 49 kW of reboil per m³/h of refluxstep 2 of 2

From the previous slide$Q_{202}=V\lambda,\qquad \Delta Q_{203}\approx\Delta L\,\lambda$
$\lambda=\dfrac{3956\times3600}{40{,}798}=349\ \mathrm{kJ/kg}$HMB: E-202 duty over stream 4 flow
$\rho_L=24{,}608/49.0=502\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$reflux meter basis, stream 5
$\dfrac{\Delta Q_{203}}{\Delta L}=\dfrac{502\times349}{3600}=48.7\ \mathrm{kW\ per\ m^3/h}$combine the two

Linear only near design; far from it tray temperatures and boil-up shift.

Interactive — reflux set point FIC-204

What each m³/h of reflux costs

From the derivation$\Delta Q_{203}=48.7\,\Delta L$

Design 49 m³/h. Product spec: C4+ in propane ≤ 2.5 mol % (AI-219); design makes 1.5 mol %.

E-203 duty, kW
steam, kg/h
CO₂, kg/h

The energy balance gives the price of reflux; only the analyzer on the OTS can say how low it may go.

Example 1.3 · problem statement

EXAMPLE 1.3Trimming the reflux giveaway

Read first

The C-201 propane product carries 1.50 mol % C4 and heavier against a specification of ≤ 2.5 mol % (AI-219). Operations propose lowering the reflux from 49 to 45 m³/h at constant feed and distillate.

Estimate the reboiler duty, the LP steam and the CO₂ saved per hour and per year (8,000 h). Use $\lambda$ and $\rho_L$ from the design case, 0.5908 kW of E-203 duty per kg/h of steam, and $EF_s=0.1474$ kg CO₂/kg.

Example 1.3 · solution

EXAMPLE 1.34 m³/h of reflux ≈ 330 kg/h of steam

Section 1-2 and 1-1$\Delta Q_{203}=\Delta L\,\rho_L\lambda,\qquad \Delta\dot E=\Delta\dot m_s EF_s$
$\Delta Q_{203}=4\times502.2\times349.1/3600=194.8\ \mathrm{kW}$reboil no longer needed
$\Delta\dot m_s=194.8/0.5908=329.7\ \mathrm{kg/h}$E-203 duty per kg/h of steam
$\Delta\dot E=329.7\times0.1474=48.6\ \mathrm{kg/h}$3.3 % of the baseline
$48.6\times8000/1000=389\ \mathrm{t\,CO_2/yr}$annual

Column pressure

Lower pressure separates more easily — until the condenser stops it

Lower pressure helps

Propane and butane differ more in volatility when colder: less reflux, same split.

The condenser limits it

The top must still condense against cooling water plus about 10 K.

Inerts add margin

Non-condensables need extra pressure above the bare dew point.

Interactive — cooling water sets the floor

How low could the top pressure go?

$$\log_{10}P^{sat}=4.53678-\dfrac{1149.36}{T+24.906}$$

Propane Antoine fit (NIST), $P$ in bar, $T$ in K, valid 277–361 K.

condensing T, °C
min. top P, bar a
design top P, bar a
18.0

Tropical cooling water near 32 °C pins the top near 15–16 bar a: the model's 15 °C water would allow far lower pressure than a Thai site can.

Pumps and drives · from Lecture 07

Throttling wastes head the pump already made

$Q$
volumetric flow
m³/s
$\Delta P$
pressure the pump adds
Pa
$\eta$
pump efficiency (P-201: 0.65, HMB)
–

$$P_{sh}=\dfrac{Q\,\Delta P}{\eta},\qquad Q\propto N,\ \ \Delta P\propto N^2,\ \ P_{sh}\propto N^3$$

A variable-speed drive (VSD) cuts speed instead of burning the excess head across FV-201.

Interactive — P-201 feed pump

Throttle valve or variable speed?

Previous slide$P_{sh}=Q\,\Delta P/\eta$

System: 1.41 MPa static + 0.15 MPa friction at 60 m³/h (assumed). Pump: 1.94 MPa at 60 m³/h, 2.25 MPa shut-off (assumed).

A VSD saves about 9 kW at design flow — under 0.5 % of the unit's CO₂, so rank it after every steam measure.

Lecture 1-2 · summary

What section 1-2 settled

  • Steam in leaves through the condenser: $Q_{201}+Q_{203}=Q_{202}+\Delta\dot H_{\mathrm{prod}}$.
  • Reflux costs about 49 kW of reboil per m³/h; trimming 4 m³/h saves 389 t/yr.
  • Cooling-water temperature sets the lowest useful top pressure.
  • A VSD on P-201 is real but small: rank steam measures first.

How much steam can heat already inside the unit replace?

Lecture 1-3 · the plan

Heat integration on one column

  1. Hot and cold streamsfour streams read from the HMB
  2. Shifted temperatures and ΔTminthe rule that keeps heat flowing downhill
  3. Composite curvesthe minimum steam and cooling targets
  4. The feed/overhead exchangerabout 0.8 MW recovered from the condenser
  5. Energy against area, and the new risksΔTmin as an economic choice; a new hazard and operability (HAZOP) node

Hot and cold streams · from the HMB design case

A −1 °C feed beside a 45 °C condenser

StreamTypeFrom → to (°C)Duty (kW)Heat-capacity flow $CP$ (kW/K)
H1 overhead vapour, stream 4hot45.0 → 39.43,956706 (mostly condensing)
C1a feed liquid, stream 2cold−1 → 661,48022.1
C1b feed vaporizingcold66 → 752,023225

From Lecture 02, Energy targeting

Shift each stream by half of ΔTminstep 1 of 2

Heat flows only from hotter to colder, and an exchanger needs a driving force. One shift builds both rules in.

$\Delta T_{min}$
smallest hot–cold temperature difference allowed in any exchanger
K
$T^*$
shifted temperature on one common scale
°C
$T^*_{hot}=T-\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta T_{min}$hot streams pulled down half the gap
$T^*_{cold}=T+\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta T_{min}$cold streams pushed up the other half

On the $T^*$ scale, a hot stream may heat any cold stream that lies below it.

From Lecture 02, Problem table

Cascade the surplus down the intervalsstep 2 of 2

$k$
temperature interval between two neighbouring $T^*$ values
–
$\Delta H_k$
net heat demand in interval $k$
kW
$Q_{H,min}$
minimum hot utility (steam)
kW
$\Delta H_k=\left(\textstyle\sum CP_{cold}-\sum CP_{hot}\right)\Delta T^*_k$energy balance on one interval
$R_k=Q_{H}-\textstyle\sum_{j\le k}\Delta H_j\ \ge 0$heat passed down must never be negative

$Q_{H,min}$ is the smallest $Q_H$ keeping every $R_k\ge0$; where $R_k=0$ is the pinch.

Interactive — composite curves of C-201

How much steam does the unit really need?

With the bottoms left alone, about 0.8 MW of steam can come from the condenser; the cold feed is the only sink below 45 °C.

Example 1.4 · problem statement

EXAMPLE 1.4A feed/overhead exchanger ahead of E-201

Read first

The feed (stream 2, 31,809 kg/h, liquid at −1 °C, $c_p=2.5$ kJ/kg·K) can be preheated by the overhead vapour (stream 4, condensing from 45.0 to 39.4 °C, 3,956 kW) in a new exchanger E-204 placed before E-201, with $\Delta T_{min}=10$ K.

  1. Find the feed outlet temperature and the duty recovered.
  2. Find the LP steam and CO₂ saved ($EF_s=0.1474$; 0.6022 kW of E-201 duty per kg/h of steam).
  3. Estimate the area for $U=500$ W/m²·K.

Example 1.4 · solution

EXAMPLE 1.4The hot end sets the feed outletstep 1 of 2

Energy balance on the feed$Q=CP_f\,(T_{f,out}-T_{f,in}),\qquad CP_f=\dot m_f c_p$
$CP_f=\dfrac{31{,}809}{3600}\times2.5=22.1\ \mathrm{kW/K}$kg/h to kg/s
$T_{f,out}=45-10=35\ \mathrm{^\circ C}$counter-current: hot inlet meets cold outlet
$Q=22.1\times(35-(-1))=795\ \mathrm{kW}$(a) recovered duty
$T_{h,out}=45-795/706=43.9\ \mathrm{^\circ C}$overhead only part-condenses; E-202 does the rest

Example 1.4 · solution

EXAMPLE 1.413 % of the unit's CO₂ for about 70 m²step 2 of 2

Section 1-1 and Lecture 06$\Delta\dot E=\Delta\dot m_s EF_s,\quad Q=UA\,\Delta T_{lm},\quad \Delta T_{lm}=\dfrac{\Delta T_2-\Delta T_1}{\ln(\Delta T_2/\Delta T_1)}$
$\Delta\dot m_s=795/0.6022=1321\ \mathrm{kg/h};\ \Delta\dot E=195\ \mathrm{kg/h}$(b) 13.2 % of 1,470
$\Delta T_1=10,\ \Delta T_2=43.9+1=44.9\Rightarrow\Delta T_{lm}=23.2\ \mathrm{K}$both terminal differences
$A=\dfrac{795\,000}{500\times23.2}=68.5\ \mathrm{m^2}$(c) area

Bonus: E-202 sheds 20 % of its duty — the condenser is the unit's maximum-feed bottleneck.

Interactive — from Lecture 06, heat-exchanger cost

Where is the economic ΔTmin?

Example 1.4$Q=CP_f\,(46-\Delta T_{min}),\quad A=Q/(U\Delta T_{lm})$

8,000 h/yr; capital annualised at 0.1168 per year (8 %, 15 yr).

With a feed this cold the optimum falls below 5 K: the practical approach of a shell-and-tube exchanger, not cost, sets the limit.

Before you build it

Every new exchanger is a new HAZOP node

Tube leak

Feed at 2.36 MPa g leaks into the 1.70 MPa g overhead: AI-219 rises.

Coupled control

Feed rate now moves the condenser load; start-up needs a bypass.

Test first

Run the change on the OTS and in HAZOP Studio before management of change (MOC).

Lecture 1-3 · summary

What section 1-3 settled

  • Shift hot streams down and cold streams up by $\Delta T_{min}/2$, then cascade.
  • The cold feed is the unit's only sink for condenser heat.
  • A 68 m² feed/overhead exchanger saves 795 kW, 13 % of the CO₂.
  • Moving heat across a unit boundary is not a saving.

1-4

Lecture 1-4

When does a heat pump on electricity cut CO₂?

Lecture 1-4 · the plan

Electrifying heat, honestly

  1. What a heat pump buysheat lifted from a cold source with electricity
  2. The Carnot ceilingthe coefficient of performance falls as the lift grows
  3. Why C-201 cannot recompress its own overheadthe lift crosses propane's critical point
  4. A heat pump on the feed preheatercondenser heat at about 40 °C lifted to 85 °C
  5. Break-even grid factorwhen electricity beats steam on CO₂

From Lecture 07, Equipment efficiency

Pay for the lift, not for the heat

Section 1-3 used all the condenser heat the cold feed can take. The rest is too cold — unless we lift it.

$Q_H$
heat delivered to the process
kW
$W$
compressor electricity
kW
$$\mathrm{COP}=\dfrac{Q_H}{W}$$

Coefficient of performance (COP); Lecture 07: typically 3–6 for waste-heat recovery.

The Carnot ceiling

Two balances give the best possible COP

$T_H,\ T_L$
condensing and evaporating temperatures of the working fluid
K
$Q_L$
heat taken from the source
kW
$\eta_{II}$
second-law efficiency: real COP over Carnot COP
–
$Q_H=Q_L+W$first law around the cycle
$Q_H/T_H=Q_L/T_L$second law, reversible cycle: no entropy made
$\mathrm{COP}_C=\dfrac{Q_H}{Q_H-Q_L}=\dfrac{T_H}{T_H-T_L}$eliminate $Q_L$; temperatures in kelvin

Real machines reach $\mathrm{COP}=\eta_{II}\,\mathrm{COP}_C$ with $\eta_{II}\approx0.4$–$0.6$.

Interactive — the lift decides

COP against temperature lift

Previous slide$\mathrm{COP}=\eta_{II}\dfrac{T_H}{T_H-T_L}$

Halving the lift roughly doubles the COP: a heat pump pays only where source and sink sit close together.

Interactive — vapour recompression (VRC)

Could C-201 compress its own top vapour into the reboiler?

VRC compresses the overhead until it condenses in the reboiler. It works on close-boiling splits.

Section 1-2, propane Antoine$\log_{10}P^{sat}=4.53678-\dfrac{1149.36}{T+24.906}$
pressure needed, bar a
ratio from 18 bar a
propane Tc
96.7 °C

Reboiling at 109 °C needs condensing near 119 °C, above propane's critical point: direct VRC is impossible on this column.

Example 1.5 · problem statement

EXAMPLE 1.5A heat pump on the feed preheater

Read first

After the feed/overhead exchanger of Example 1.4, E-201 still supplies 2,708 kW to heat the feed from 35 to 75 °C. A closed-cycle heat pump could take this heat from the overhead (evaporating at 32 °C) and deliver it by condensing at 85 °C, with $\eta_{II}=0.50$.

  1. Find the COP.
  2. Find the compressor electricity.
  3. Find the net change in CO₂ with $EF_g=0.4750$ kg CO₂e/kWh, if the steam it replaces carries 0.2448 kg CO₂ per kWh of E-201 duty.

Example 1.5 · solution

EXAMPLE 1.5COP 3.4, about 0.8 MW of electricitystep 1 of 2

Carnot slide$\mathrm{COP}=\eta_{II}\dfrac{T_H}{T_H-T_L},\qquad W=Q_H/\mathrm{COP}$
$\mathrm{COP}_C=\dfrac{358.15}{358.15-305.15}=6.76$85 °C and 32 °C in kelvin
$\mathrm{COP}=0.50\times6.76=3.38$(a)
$W=2708/3.38=801\ \mathrm{kW}$(b) compressor power
$Q_L=2708-801=1907\ \mathrm{kW}$also taken off E-202's load

Example 1.5 · solution

EXAMPLE 1.5Net cut of 282 kg CO₂e/hstep 2 of 2

Section 1-1$EF_{heat}=\dfrac{EF_s}{0.6022}=\dfrac{0.1474}{0.6022}=0.2448\ \mathrm{kg/kWh}$
$+W\,EF_g=801\times0.4750=381\ \mathrm{kg/h}$CO₂ added in the grid
$-Q_H\,EF_{heat}=2708\times0.2448=663\ \mathrm{kg/h}$CO₂ removed with the steam
$\Delta\dot E=381-663=-282\ \mathrm{kg/h}$(c) 19 % of the 1,470 baseline

Temperatures are assumed design values; a real cycle needs a working fluid and compressor check.

Interactive — grid factor against COP

When does the heat pump stop paying in CO₂?

Example 1.5$\Delta\dot E=Q_H\left(\dfrac{EF_g}{\mathrm{COP}}-EF_{heat}\right)$

Break-even is $\mathrm{COP}^*=EF_g/EF_{heat}\approx1.9$ on today's grid: a low-lift heat pump wins now; with solar power it wins by far more.

Lecture 1-4 · summary

What section 1-4 settled

  • $\mathrm{COP}=\eta_{II}T_H/(T_H-T_L)$: the lift sets what a heat pump can do.
  • Direct recompression fails on C-201: 119 °C is above propane's critical point.
  • A 32 → 85 °C heat pump on the feed cuts about 282 kg/h net.
  • It pays in CO₂ only while COP exceeds $EF_g/EF_{heat}$.

1-5

Lecture 1-5

How do we decarbonize the steam and power the unit buys?

Lecture 1-5 · the plan

Lower the factor, not the flow

  1. Boiler efficiencyexcess air and stack temperature set the losses
  2. Fuel switchingbiomass, oil, coal and hydrogen blends compared on one scale
  3. Hydrogen blends20 vol % hydrogen cuts only about 7 % of the CO₂
  4. Clean electricitygreen power contracts, and why an electric boiler needs them
  5. Capture at the stackwhat carbon capture costs in heat

From Lecture 09, Fuel combustion

Too little air wastes fuel; too much heats the sky

Sections 1-2 to 1-4 cut the kg of steam. Now we cut the CO₂ in each kg.

Excess air completes combustion; every extra kg of it leaves the stack hot.

Measure (Lecture 09)Efficiency gain
Excess-air control1–3 %
Oxygen-enriched air0–10 %
Air preheater on flue gas5–15 %
Convection-section upgrade3–5 %
Furnace coating1–3 %

A field formula for stack loss

Siegert's formula: two readings, one loss

$q_A$
flue-gas (stack) loss, share of fuel heat
%
$T_{fg},\ T_a$
stack and combustion-air temperatures
°C
$O_2$
oxygen in dry flue gas
vol %
$A_1,\ B$
fuel constants: natural gas 0.66 and 0.009
–
$$q_A=(T_{fg}-T_a)\left(\dfrac{A_1}{21-O_2}+B\right)$$

$21-O_2$ shrinks as excess air grows, so $q_A$ rises; constants from the German flue-gas rules (1. BImSchV).

Interactive — the site boiler

Oxygen trim and stack temperature

Previous slide$q_A=(T_{fg}-T_a)\left(\dfrac{0.66}{21-O_2}+0.009\right)$

Air 30 °C. Reference: O₂ 3 %, 180 °C ↔ $\eta_b=0.88$; other losses held fixed.

stack loss, %
boiler efficiency
C-201 steam CO₂, kg/h

An economiser that drops the stack 60 K saves more than trimming O₂ from 6 to 3 %: stack temperature is the bigger lever.

Interactive — fuel switching

The same steam, five different fuels

Section 1-1$EF_s=\dfrac{\Delta h_s}{\eta_b}\,EF_f\,f_{fossil}$

IPCC 2006 (kg CO₂/GJ): gas 56.1, oil 77.4, coal 94.6; biomass CO₂ is biogenic.

Coal steam carries 1.8 times the CO₂ of gas steam, while blending hydrogen by volume moves the factor far less than its percentage suggests.

Example 1.6 · problem statement

EXAMPLE 1.6A 20 vol % hydrogen blend in the boiler fuel

Read first

The site boiler burns natural gas (taken as methane). A supplier offers to blend 20 vol % green hydrogen into the fuel. Using volumetric lower heating values of 35.8 MJ/Nm³ for CH₄ and 10.8 MJ/Nm³ for H₂, find (a) the share of boiler heat still supplied by methane and (b) the cut in the CO₂ of C-201's steam, baseline 1,416 kg/h, at unchanged boiler efficiency.

Example 1.6 · solution

EXAMPLE 1.6Hydrogen is light: 20 % by volume is 7 % by energy

$$f_{CH_4}=\dfrac{(1-x)\,LHV_{CH_4}}{(1-x)\,LHV_{CH_4}+x\,LHV_{H_2}}$$

$x$ = hydrogen volume fraction; $f_{CH_4}$ = share of heat from methane, the only CO₂ source.

$f_{CH_4}=\dfrac{0.8(35.8)}{0.8(35.8)+0.2(10.8)}=\dfrac{28.64}{30.80}=0.930$(a) 93 % of the heat
$\Delta\dot E=(1-0.930)\times1416=99\ \mathrm{kg/h}$(b) a 7.0 % cut

Clean electricity

An electric boiler on today's grid doubles the steam's CO₂

Section 1-1$EF_s=\Delta h_s\,EF_f/\eta_b=0.1474\ \mathrm{kg/kg},\qquad \dot E_e=P_e\,EF_g$
$w=\dfrac{2312}{0.99\times3600}=0.649\ \mathrm{kWh/kg}$electric boiler, 99 % efficient
$EF_{s,el}=0.649\times0.4750=0.308\ \mathrm{kg/kg}$2.1 times gas-fired steam
$EF_g^*=0.1474/0.649=0.227\ \mathrm{kg/kWh}$grid factor needed to break even

A solar power purchase agreement (PPA) or renewable energy certificates (RECs) clear the pumps first.

From Lectures 10 and 12

Carbon capture pays for itself in heat

Carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) keeps the fuel but removes CO₂ from the flue gas.

$q_{reg}$
solvent regeneration heat per tonne captured, 30 wt % amine (typical)
GJ/t
$w_c$
compression power per tonne captured (typical)
kWh/t
$$\dfrac{\Delta m_{net}}{m_{cap}}=1-\dfrac{q_{reg}\,EF_f}{\eta_b}-w_c\,EF_g$$
$=1-\dfrac{3.5(0.0561)}{0.88}-0.1(0.475)$3.5 GJ/t, 100 kWh/t; $EF_f$ in t/GJ
$=1-0.223-0.048=0.73$about a quarter is spent on capture

Lecture 1-5 · summary

What section 1-5 settled

  • Stack temperature and flue-gas O₂ set the boiler's loss (Siegert).
  • Fuel choice moves the steam factor; hydrogen by volume moves it little.
  • Electric steam needs a grid below about 0.23 kg/kWh.
  • Capture keeps about 73 % of what it catches after paying for heat and compression.

1-6

Lecture 1-6

Which options first? Ranking by cost per tonne avoided

Lecture 1-6 · the plan

From a list of ideas to a roadmap

  1. Cost per tonne avoidedthe marginal abatement cost of one measure
  2. Annualising capitalthe capital recovery factor turns capital expenditure (CAPEX) into THB per year
  3. Options interactthe order of building changes every measure's tonnes
  4. The C-201 curve and roadmapcheap tonnes first, then the carbon-price line
  5. From slide to plantOTS test, HAZOP, cost estimate, footprint report

Cost per tonne avoided

One number to rank unlike measures

Sections 1-2 to 1-5 gave tonnes. Ranking them also needs money, on one common basis.

$\mathrm{MAC}$
marginal abatement cost: net cost per tonne CO₂e avoided
THB/t
$C_{cap}$
capital expenditure (CAPEX), installed
THB
$\Delta C_{op}$
change in yearly operating cost (OPEX); savings negative
THB/yr
$\Delta m$
CO₂e avoided per year
t/yr
$$\mathrm{MAC}=\dfrac{\mathrm{CRF}\cdot C_{cap}+\Delta C_{op}}{\Delta m}$$

Negative MAC: the measure saves money and CO₂ together. THB = Thai baht.

Annualising capital

The capital recovery factor (CRF)

$i$
discount rate
1/yr
$n$
project life
yr
$A$
equal yearly payment that repays $C_{cap}$
THB/yr
$C_{cap}=\textstyle\sum_{t=1}^{n}\dfrac{A}{(1+i)^t}=A\,\dfrac{(1+i)^n-1}{i(1+i)^n}$present value of $n$ payments; geometric sum
$\mathrm{CRF}=\dfrac{A}{C_{cap}}=\dfrac{i(1+i)^n}{(1+i)^n-1}$invert: payment per baht of capital
$i=0.08,\ n=15\ \Rightarrow\ \mathrm{CRF}=0.1168\ \mathrm{yr^{-1}}$the value used in this deck

Example 1.7 · problem statement

EXAMPLE 1.7The cost per tonne of the feed/overhead exchanger

Read first

The feed/overhead exchanger of Example 1.4 saves 1,321 kg/h of LP steam and 194.7 kg/h of CO₂ for 8,000 h/yr. Its installed cost is taken as 12 million THB (a placeholder until it is sized in CAPEX Studio), with maintenance at 3 % of CAPEX per year. Steam costs 0.996 THB/kg (natural gas 400 THB/MMBtu). Take $i=8$ %, $n=15$ yr. Find the marginal abatement cost.

ItemValue
Steam saved1,321 kg/h
CO₂ avoided194.7 kg/h
Operating hours8,000 h/yr
CAPEX12.0 MTHB
Maintenance3 %/yr of CAPEX
Steam price0.996 THB/kg
CRF (8 %, 15 yr)0.1168

Example 1.7 · solution

EXAMPLE 1.7−5,600 THB per tonne: it pays to cut

MAC and CRF slides$\mathrm{MAC}=\dfrac{\mathrm{CRF}\cdot C_{cap}+\Delta C_{op}}{\Delta m}$
$\mathrm{CRF}\cdot C_{cap}+0.03\,C_{cap}=1.40+0.36=1.76\ \mathrm{MTHB/yr}$capital plus maintenance
$\Delta C_{op}=-1321\times8000\times0.996=-10.53\ \mathrm{MTHB/yr}$steam no longer bought
$\Delta m=194.7\times8000/1000=1558\ \mathrm{t/yr}$tonnes avoided
$\mathrm{MAC}=(1.76-10.53)\times10^6/1558=-5{,}630\ \mathrm{THB/t}$simple payback about 1.2 years

Options interact

Evaluate each measure on what is left

Shrinking duty

After the feed/overhead exchanger, the heat pump replaces 2,708 kW, not 3,503.

Cleaner input

Green power makes the heat pump's electricity zero-carbon, so its tonnes grow.

Double counting

Summing tonnes measured against the original baseline overstates the total.

Bar width is tonnes, height is THB/t: every bar below the carbon-price line costs less than the carbon it avoids.

Four checks before a measure is real

  2. HAZOP Studiohazard and operability study of the new node; MOC record
  3. CAPEX Studioreplace every placeholder cost with a sized estimate

Lecture 1-6 · summary

What section 1-6 settled

  • MAC = (CRF · CAPEX + ΔOPEX) / tonnes; negative means it pays.
  • The feed/overhead exchanger costs about −5,600 THB/t.
  • Evaluate measures in building order to avoid double counting.
  • Test on the OTS and HAZOP before any measure is committed.

Problem 1.1 · statement · read first

PROBLEM 1.1The baseline at maximum feed

Read first

The maximum-feed case of the C-201 HMB runs 70 m³/h of feed with the reflux ratioed to it. Using the data in the table, $EF_s=0.1474$ kg CO₂/kg, $EF_g=0.4750$ kg CO₂e/kWh, motor efficiency 0.93 and a 38.7 kW cooling-water pump, find (a) the emission rate, (b) the intensity per tonne of feed, and (c) compare it with the design case, 46.2 kg/t.

Maximum-feed case (HMB)Value
Feed, stream 137,111 kg/h
Steam to E-201, stream 96,902 kg/h
Steam to E-203, stream 104,389 kg/h
P-201A shaft54.1 kW
P-202A shaft21.7 kW
Reflux57.2 m³/h

Problem 1.1 · solution

PROBLEM 1.1The intensity barely moves with throughput

Example 1.2$\dot E=\dot m_s\,EF_s+P_e\,EF_g$
$(6902+4389)\times0.1474=1664\ \mathrm{kg/h}$steam
$\left(\dfrac{54.1+21.7}{0.93}+38.7\right)0.4750=57.1\ \mathrm{kg/h}$power
$\dot E=1721\ \mathrm{kg/h};\ \ I=1721/37.111=46.4\ \mathrm{kg/t}$(a), (b)

(c) Within 0.5 % of design: reflux is ratioed to feed, so steam scales with throughput.

At turndown (40 m³/h feed) the HMB ratios the reflux to 32.7 m³/h. (a) Find the turndown intensity from the table, with the same factors as Problem 1.1. (b) Operators instead leave the reflux at the design 49 m³/h. Using 48.7 kW of reboil per m³/h of reflux and 0.5908 kW per kg/h of steam, find the extra CO₂ and the new intensity.

Problem 1.2 · solution

PROBLEM 1.2A fixed reflux adds 20 % at turndown

Section 1-2$\Delta Q_{203}=48.7\,\Delta L,\qquad \Delta\dot E=\Delta\dot m_s EF_s$
$6319(0.1474)+\left(\tfrac{52.5}{0.93}+38.7\right)0.475=931+45=977\ \mathrm{kg/h}$(a) 46.1 kg/t

Repeat Example 1.4 with $\Delta T_{min}=5$ K. Find the duty, the area ($U=500$ W/m²·K), and the extra steam, CO₂ and area compared with the 10 K design. Comment on whether the extra area is worth it, using the trade-off slide of section 1-3.

Problem 1.3 · solution

PROBLEM 1.3+110 kW for +31 m²

Example 1.4$Q=CP_f(46-\Delta T_{min}),\quad A=\dfrac{Q}{U\,\Delta T_{lm}}$

The heat pump of Example 1.5 delivers 2,708 kW to the feed. The site signs a solar power purchase agreement with a contracted factor of 0.10 kg CO₂e/kWh, and a cheaper compressor gives COP 3.0. Problem 1.5 · how to set it up

PROBLEM 1.5A step test, not a guess

  1. Startload the design initial condition; TIC-208 in automatic mode; settle 20 min
  2. Steplower the FIC-204 set point 1 m³/h every 20 min of simulated time
  3. Stopwhen AI-219 reaches 2.3 mol %, AI-220 exceeds 2.0, or a flood alarm sounds
  4. Reporttable of reflux, FI-205, AI-219, AI-220; CO₂ with $EF_s=0.1474$ and steam at 0.996 THB/kg

Before you leave

Key Takeaways

1

Count first: steam is 96 % of C-201's footprint.

2

Stop giveaway: each m³/h of reflux costs about 49 kW of reboil.

3

Recover before you buy: the cold feed takes 0.8 MW from the overhead.

4

Electrify only where COP beats $EF_g/EF_{heat}$, and check the lift.

5

Rank by MAC in building order; prove each step on the OTS.
